text.hook:
"RAII means destructors clean up."
True, until the exception is never caught.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Lifetime is ownership
2. What stack unwinding really runs
3. Why destructors must not throw
4. Writing your own RAII wrapper
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Ownership, stack unwinding and exception safety: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: The object's lifetime **is** the ownership

cards.label: Constructor
cards.text: Acquires the resource, or **throws**. A half-acquired object never exists.

cards.label: Destructor
cards.text: Releases it, on every exit path: return, break, exception.

slides.takeaway: No naked `new`/`delete`, no manual `lock()`/`unlock()`. Every resource is owned by an object from the moment it is acquired.

slides.title: A resource is anything you must give back
slides.takeaway: A forgotten `unlock()` is worse than a leak: every other thread blocks forever.

slides.title: When do local destructors actually run?
slides.takeaway: Want guaranteed cleanup? Put a top-level `catch (...)` in `main` and in every thread function.

slides.title: Destructors must not throw

cards.label: Implicitly noexcept (C++11)
cards.text: A `throw` from a destructor calls `std::terminate`, even inside `try`/`catch`.

cards.label: But release can fail
cards.text: Offer an explicit `close()` that throws or returns an error. The destructor closes only if still open, and logs.

slides.takeaway: Even with `noexcept(false)`, a throw during unwinding of another exception is `std::terminate`.

slides.title: RAII wrapper for a raw handle
items: Constructor acquires or throws: no "zombie" object
Destructor releases, `noexcept`, handles the empty state
Decide copying: move-only, deep copy (`dup()`) or shared
slides.warn: The generated copy copies the handle value: two owners, a double close.

slides.lead: Members die in reverse order. Declare a `jthread` after the queue it uses, a statement handle after its connection.

items.truth: It is about any acquire/release pair: locks, files, sockets, threads.

items.myth: "RAII means the stack instead of the heap."
items.truth: The *owner* is usually automatic. The resource is often still on the heap.

items.myth: "Destructors always run when an exception is thrown."
items.truth: Only if it is caught. Uncaught: `std::terminate`, and GCC does not unwind.

items.myth: "`File(int fd)` owns the fd because it stores it."
items.truth: Ownership is a documented contract. The generated copy happily creates a second owner.
It unlocks the mutex. The mutex lives on.
It skips automatic objects. Only statics and thread-locals are destroyed.

slides.hero:
Every resource:
owned by an object
from the moment
it is acquired.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
One raw pointer, one unique_ptr, one stack object.
Then an early return.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: What does it print, and which object leaks?

slides.title:
`handle(true)` prints `+A+B+C`.
What comes next?

bullets: Early return destroys locals in reverse order: `c` (`-C`), then `b`, which deletes B (`-B`).
The raw pointer `a` is destroyed too, but destroying a pointer does nothing.
`delete a;` is a statement. A path that skips it never runs it.
slides.wrong: "`-A` at the end, the pointer goes out of scope"

slides.title: Give every resource an owner
slides.takeaway: No `delete` statement to forget: every exit path releases everything, in reverse order.

text.hook:
Lock, work, unlock. Three lines. It passed code review.
Then one bad input made the work throw.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The exception is caught. So everything is fine afterwards. Right?

slides.title: `parse()` throws. Output?

slides.verdict: D. `0`: the lock is still held
slides.verdict_sub: The exception is caught, but `m` is still locked by main
bullets: `parse()` throws, so `m.unlock()` never runs. Catching the exception does not undo that.
`try_lock` fails: the mutex is still owned. (The full program unlocks it in main before exit.)
With `m.lock()` instead, the thread blocks forever: a hang, no crash, no message.
Test from another thread on purpose: relocking a `std::mutex` from its owner is UB.
slides.wrong: "`1`, the stack unwinds and releases the lock"

slides.title: Put the unlock in a destructor
slides.takeaway: Manual `lock()`/`unlock()` around code that can throw is a lock waiting to be lost. Ownership must be an RAII object.

text.hook:
The constructor throws. The caller catches it.
The destructor right there frees raw_.
So nothing leaks. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.

slides.title: Caught. What leaks?

slides.verdict_sub: Prints only `caught`. LeakSanitizer: "Direct leak of 400 byte(s)"
bullets: The constructor never completed, so the object never existed: `~Holder` does **not** run.
Every fully constructed member and base is destroyed, in reverse order.
`safe_` frees its buffer. `raw_` is a raw pointer: its destructor releases nothing.
With `new Holder`, the new-expression also frees the object's own memory.

slides.title: One resource per RAII member
slides.takeaway: Constructor failure destroys finished members, never the object itself. Throwing is still the right way to report it.

text.hook:
"This function gives the basic exception guarantee."
It just threw. What do you actually know?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: "Exception safe" has four levels. Interviewers expect you to name them.

slides.title: `add_all` throws. What is in `out`?

slides.verdict_sub: Basic guarantee: invariants hold, values may have changed
bullets: Each `push_back` is **strong**: the failed 3rd one left `out` as it was.
The loop as a whole is only **basic**: orders 1 and 2 stay in.
Each level includes the weaker ones. RAII gets you basic, design gets you strong.

slides.title: Work on a copy, commit with a no-throw swap
slides.takeaway: Strong is built from no-throw steps. It costs a copy, so libraries choose it only where it is cheap or essential.
